My Summer with PCIe and SISCI (Reference Draft)
Purpose of this document
This is a working reference summary of what I accomplished over the summer using Dolphin PCIe technology and SISCI software. It is written for thesis planning and chapter development, not as final chapter prose.

Executive summary
Over the summer, I progressed from basic node access and installer execution to full cluster-level diagnosis, performance validation, and early application development on top of SISCI. The work combined three tracks:

Platform engineering: bring-up, recovery, and stabilization of multi-node PCIe systems.
Performance engineering: validating link health, benchmarking latency/throughput, and isolating bottlenecks.
Applied development and documentation: building SISCI-based prototypes and producing customer-ready technical guidance.
By the end of the period, I had repeatedly demonstrated practical competence in remote cluster operations, ExpressWare/SISCI troubleshooting, link-level PCIe diagnostics, and communication of technical findings to both internal and customer-facing audiences.

Timeline of work and progression
Phase 1: Initial bring-up and installer workflow validation
Key activities:

Connected to remote nodes over SSH.
Identified OS/kernel versions and installer compatibility constraints.
Copied installers, corrected execution gaps, and completed firmware/EEPROM update cycles.
Used diagnostic commands to validate software and hardware state.
Important progression:

Early in the process, installer files had been copied but not actually executed. I caught and corrected this by enforcing executable permissions and explicit installer runs.
I established a repeatable baseline sequence: transfer, install, firmware check, reset, reboot, re-verify.
What this phase produced:

A reliable procedural baseline for first-pass SISCI/ExpressWare deployment and validation.
Phase 2: Root-cause troubleshooting and cluster recovery
Key activities:

Investigated lane-width degradation (x8 when x16 was expected).
Cross-checked dis_diag and firmware outputs between nodes.
Escalated from software-only assumptions to physical layer inspection.
Found and corrected hardware connection issues (unplugged cable) that software tuning alone could not fix.
Important progression:

This phase was where diagnosis became systematic: verify, hypothesize, isolate, retest.
I learned to treat PCIe health as a full-stack problem (physical cabling, adapter state, firmware partition, driver/kernel alignment, and host config).
What this phase produced:

Restored x16 operation and active partition health across nodes.
A practical lesson for thesis discussion: many "software" interconnect problems are ultimately cross-layer.
Phase 3: OS/kernel alignment and compatibility hardening
Key activities:

Standardized nodes onto compatible Linux families and kernel lines.
Repeated install/reinstall with RT and non-RT variants.
Used local console and USB recovery workflows when remote operations were insufficient.
Escalated to BIOS/firmware support when symptoms indicated lower-level instability.
Important progression:

I documented that repeated failed installs are often secondary symptoms; the true blocker can be kernel/driver mismatch or firmware-level instability.
What this phase produced:

Matched OS/kernel baselines on the Genfi nodes.
A clearer compatibility model for future deployments.
Phase 4: Stable diagnostics and benchmark-driven validation
Key activities:

Confirmed both nodes visible in topology with valid sessions.
Verified clean health reports (no warnings/errors) with x16 Gen4 links.
Ran and interpreted benchmark tools for throughput and latency.
Benchmark and measurement exposure:

DMA_Bench: throughput-oriented transfer behavior.
SCIBench2 / SCIPP / SCIMemcopyBench / interrupt benchmark: latency and transfer-behavior perspectives.
Example latency ranges captured in notes (microseconds):
DMA_Bench: about 36.04 to 38.81 us.
SCIBench2: about 3.85 to 3.98 us.
SCIPP: about 1.0359 to 2.736 us.
SCIMemcopy: around 3.72 us.
Interrupt bench: about 4.92 to 5.001 us.
What this phase produced:

A practical benchmarking workflow for diagnosis and tuning.
Evidence for thesis sections on method, instrumentation, and performance interpretation.
Phase 5: Switch integration, constraints, and operational lessons
Key activities:

Integrated a switch into a two-node path.
Observed throughput drop and investigated cause.
Determined speed fallback behavior due to generation mismatch (Gen4 adapters routed through Gen3 switch).
Noted recurring dmesg errors when config expectations (Gen4) did not match effective switch behavior (Gen3 path).
Important progression:

Learned that cluster configuration files and expected link parameters must track real hardware capabilities after topology changes.
Established the need to regenerate config and validate post-change state whenever switching fabric design changes.
What this phase produced:

A concrete case study of topology-induced performance limits.
Useful thesis material for "expected vs. effective bandwidth" analysis.
Phase 6: Customer support engineering and technical communication
Key activities:

Worked customer ticket workflows (including Fujitsu follow-up).
Produced structured technical responses on:
host identification limits in network-less PCIe contexts,
dummy/static IP interface requirements,
dishosts and node manager behavior,
kernel module mismatch symptoms,
install-time SSH dependency versus runtime proprietary port behavior.
Reduced support noise by requesting minimum diagnostic evidence first.
Important progression:

Transitioned from local troubleshooting to externally consumable guidance.
Improved response quality by separating tested facts from "needs validation" claims.
What this phase produced:

A support-oriented knowledge base and reproducible verification checklists.
Strong thesis material on operationalization and field support practices.
Phase 7: SISCI application prototyping and demo engineering
Key activities:

Designed and planned a two-node SISCI "vanishing text" chat app.
Defined shared-memory architecture elements:
presence heartbeat segment,
append-only key-event ring with sequence and expiration.
Broke implementation into staged phases (scaffold, presence, transport, vanish logic, terminal UI).
Continued adapting existing demos from three-node assumptions to two-node constraints.
Captured SmartIO device-lending demo flow for camera/video use cases (add, connect, mark available, borrow, return, cleanup).
Important progression:

Moved from using the platform to designing software that exploits SISCI semantics directly.
What this phase produced:

Chapter-ready material connecting low-level transport properties to application behavior and UX constraints.
Phase 8: Expansion and inventory testing methodology
Key activities:

Produced a reproducible PCIe expansion box detection method:
baseline lspci capture,
post-install capture,
diff generation,
custom filter pass to isolate truly new devices versus renumbered entries.
Packaged this into a formal report workflow with reproducibility notes.
What this phase produced:

A clean test methodology suitable for thesis appendices and future lab validation.
Major technical outcomes
Built a repeatable SISCI/ExpressWare installation and recovery process across remote nodes.
Restored and validated high-quality link state (x16 Gen4) and session integrity in a two-node topology.
Established benchmark-informed diagnosis habits for throughput and latency problems.
Identified and documented hardware-generation mismatch effects on effective performance.
Produced support-grade explanations for cluster formation, driver mismatch symptoms, and deployment prerequisites.
Designed an original SISCI application architecture that demonstrates shared-memory and event-distribution concepts.
Created a reproducible PCIe device-detection testing pipeline for expansion scenarios.

Chapter seed B: Multi-layer diagnosis of PCIe performance

Chapter seed D: Operationalization and support engineering

Chapter seed E: Expansion and device discovery methodology
Focus:

Repeatable lspci diff/filter pipeline.
Distinguishing true device additions from enumeration renumbering.
